answers.explanation: An A record is the plain name-to-address mapping.
"Quad A", because an IPv6 address is 128 bits, four times the 32 bits in an A record.
A record's TTL controls caching. Lower it before you move a server, so the old address doesn't linger for days.
Same name, different job: in DNS it's a number of seconds that a record may be cached.
The canonical name is the real one; the CNAME's own name is the nickname.
That's the point of aliases: everything that points at host1 follows it automatically.
A CNAME stands for the whole name, so nothing else may sit beside it. That's why the bare domain, which needs NS and SOA records, usually can't be a CNAME.
Clients usually try the first address, so rotating the order spreads them across the servers.
NS records also do the delegating, as in the hierarchy lesson.
